whyItExists.problem: Without indexes, MongoDB scans every document in a collection to find matches — a COLLSCAN. On a 10-million-document collection, a query that takes 50ms with an index can take 30 seconds without one. As data grows, unindexed queries become unusable.
whyItExists.solution: Indexes are B-tree data structures that store a sorted subset of field values and pointers to documents. MongoDB can use them to jump directly to matching documents instead of scanning everything. The right indexes turn slow queries into fast ones.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Create indexes on fields you filter, sort, or use in $lookup joins. Use compound indexes for multi-field queries. Use unique indexes for natural keys like email. Use TTL indexes for auto-expiry. Use text indexes for full-text search.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Every index slows writes (the index must be updated on every insert/update/delete) and uses storage. Don't create indexes you don't need. Don't index low-cardinality fields (like a boolean) — the selectivity is too low to help. Use explain() to verify an index is actually being used.

explainModes.beginner: An index is like the index at the back of a book. Instead of reading every page to find a topic, you look up the word in the index and jump straight to the right page. MongoDB indexes do the same — instead of scanning all 1 million documents, MongoDB jumps straight to the ones you need.
explainModes.simple: An index is a sorted data structure that lets MongoDB find documents without scanning the whole collection. createIndex({ email: 1 }) creates an ascending index on the email field. The 1 means ascending, -1 means descending.
explainModes.standard: MongoDB uses B-tree indexes. A single-field index covers queries filtering on that one field. A compound index covers queries filtering on multiple indexed fields — the order of fields in the compound index matters (the ESR rule: Equality first, Sort second, Range last). Use explain() to verify query plans.
explainModes.technical: MongoDB's query planner uses an ixscan + fetch strategy for indexed queries: scan the index B-tree to find matching keys, then fetch documents by their record IDs. Covered queries avoid the fetch step entirely — when all queried fields are in the index. Compound index field order determines which prefixes are usable: { a: 1, b: 1, c: 1 } covers queries on (a), (a,b), or (a,b,c) but not (b) alone.
explainModes.deepDive: MongoDB's WiredTiger storage engine maintains indexes as separate B+ trees alongside collection data. Each index entry contains the indexed field value(s) plus the document's RecordId. The query planner runs multiple candidate plans in a 'trial period' (up to 101 documents), caches the winner per query shape in the plan cache, and invalidates it on collection rebuild or significant data change. Covered queries bypass the document fetch entirely — only the index pages are read, reducing I/O dramatically for read-heavy workloads.

content.text: Without an index, MongoDB performs a COLLSCAN (collection scan) — reading every document to find matches. With an index, MongoDB does an IXSCAN (index scan) — jumping directly to matching documents. The difference between these two for large collections can be the difference between milliseconds and minutes.
The ESR Rule for Compound Indexes
When building compound indexes, follow the ESR rule: put Equality fields first, Sort fields second, Range fields last. This ordering makes compound indexes most efficient.

A compound index (a, b, c) can serve queries that use any LEFT PREFIX: (a), (a,b), or (a,b,c). It cannot serve queries starting with b or c alone. Design your compound indexes to cover your most common query patterns.

Every index slows write operations (insert, update, delete) because all indexes must be updated for every write. A collection with 10 indexes takes ~10x more time to insert into than the same collection with 0 indexes. Only create indexes you actually query against.

questions.question: What does COLLSCAN mean in an explain() output?
options: A fast collection scan using the cache
MongoDB scanned every document in the collection (no index used)
A compressed scan of the collection
A covered query using the collection's index
questions.explanation: COLLSCAN means MongoDB read every document in the collection to find matches. This is slow for large collections and signals you need an index on the filtered fields.

questions.question: In the ESR rule for compound indexes, what does the 'S' stand for?
questions.explanation: ESR = Equality first, Sort second, Range last. Sort fields go in the middle of the compound index to allow MongoDB to satisfy the sort from the index without an extra in-memory sort step.

questions.question: A compound index on { a: 1, b: 1, c: 1 } can efficiently serve which query?
questions.explanation: Compound indexes follow the left-prefix rule — they serve queries using any left prefix. { a: 1, b: 1, c: 1 } covers queries on (a), (a,b), or (a,b,c). Queries starting with b or c alone cannot use this index.

faq.q: How many indexes should a collection have?
faq.a: Create only the indexes your queries actually need. Use explain() to verify index usage, and use $indexStats to find unused indexes. A good rule: 5–10 indexes per collection is typical; more than 15 starts to hurt write performance noticeably.

faq.q: Does MongoDB always use an index if one exists?
faq.a: No. MongoDB's query planner chooses the fastest plan. If the index is not selective enough (e.g., a boolean field with 50% true), MongoDB may choose a COLLSCAN. Use explain() to see which plan was chosen and hint() to force a specific index.

A covered query is one where all fields in the query filter AND the projection are in the index — MongoDB never reads the actual document. For example, createIndex({ email: 1, name: 1 }) covers find({ email: ... }, { name: 1, _id: 0 }). Covered queries are the fastest possible queries in MongoDB.

usedIn: Unique constraints for email and username fields
TTL indexes for session and cache expiry
examples: { email: 1 } unique index: findOne by email drops from 300ms to 1ms on 1M users
{ userId: 1, placedAt: -1 } compound index: paginated order history query uses IXSCAN instead of COLLSCAN
{ createdAt: 1 } TTL index: session documents auto-delete after 24 hours without a cleanup job
